Oh, it's... it's just the worst feeling in the world. Honestly. While I'm actually eating, it's almost like I'm in this weird trance, you know? The apartment is completely quiet, my monitors are glowing, and I'm just sort of checked out. But the second I stop—usually when the food is finally gone and I look down and actually see all the empty containers and wrappers scattered everywhere, across my desk, stacked up on the coffee table—it all just comes crashing down on me.

What is actually wrong with you?' It's this heavy, overwhelming wave of shame that just kind of washes over my whole body. I feel so pathetic and... and weak. 

And then my mind just starts racing. I start calculating how much money I just spent on all that food and the delivery fees—which are honestly ridiculous right now, they upcharge for everything, but in the moment I don't even care, I just blindly click order. But afterward, the guilt about the money mixes with the guilt about the food, and I just end up lying in bed in the dark, completely miserable. I'll replay the whole night in my head, just tossing and turning. I just don't understand why I can't have a normal dinner like everyone else. It leaves me feeling so completely defeated, and that feeling just lingers, you know? It just bleeds into the whole next day and ruins my morning, too.

I... you know, that's another one of those things where the lines just get so blurry for me. Because, okay, what does "sad or emotional" really look like, right? Like, am I sitting on my couch crying over a breakup or a movie and then ordering a pizza? Not really. But am I feeling sad *because* I'm stressed? Absolutely. 

Like, when I'm in the middle of one of those awful crunches, and it's 1 AM, and I'm looking at my screen, there's this deep, heavy feeling of just... loneliness, I guess? Or maybe it's self-pity? I start thinking about how all my friends are asleep, or how they spent their evening out at a nice dinner while I was stuck staring at vector graphics. And that makes me feel incredibly sad and isolated. It's this overwhelming sense of, "Is this really what my life is? Just working and sleeping?" And that's usually right around the time I pull up the delivery app. 

So, am I eating because I'm sad, or am I eating because I'm stressed about the deadline that's causing the sadness? It's like this tangled knot. I remember last month, it was my mom's birthday, and I had to cancel going to her dinner because a client needed emergency revisions on a pitch deck. I was so upset, just crying at my desk while I was working, and I ended up eating, I don't even know, a massive amount of Chinese takeout and a whole pint of ice cream. But again, was that because I was sad about missing the birthday, or stressed about the pitch deck? They just bleed into each other so much. I don't think I've ever just been purely sad, like on a random Tuesday with no work pressure, and turned to food. It's always wrapped up in the work, the isolation of the work, and the emotions that come from feeling trapped by it. So, I don't really know how to separate the sadness from the stress, if that makes any sense at all.

It's this heavy, overwhelming wave of shame that just kind of washes over my whole body. I feel so pathetic and... and weak. \n\nAnd then my mind just starts racing. I start calculating how much money I just spent on all that food and the delivery fees—which are honestly ridiculous right now, they upcharge for everything, but in the moment I don't even care, I just blindly click order. I'll replay the whole night in my head, just tossing and turning. I just don't understand why I can't have a normal dinner like everyone else. It leaves me feeling so completely defeated, and that feeling just lingers, you know? It's not like I'm just casually staying up until 2 AM tweaking a font or playing with color palettes for fun, you know? I just haven't paid enough attention to whether it happens outside of those crazy design crunches. I... no. No, I don't feel like I have control at all. And that's honestly the most terrifying part of the whole experience, if I'm being completely honest with you. 

When I first start, maybe there's this tiny, fleeting illusion of control. Like, I'll tell myself as I'm setting everything up at my desk that I'm only going to eat half of the noodles and I'll save the rest for lunch tomorrow. I'll even leave the lids on some of the containers, like that's going to stop me. But then... once I actually start eating, there's this very distinct point where everything just shifts. 

It's almost like an out-of-body experience. Once I start, there's this point where I'm literally just watching myself keep clicking back to the food, or reaching out and tearing open another plastic package, and my internal monologue is completely disconnected from what my body is doing. I'm sitting there actively thinking, "I should stop. I really need to stop right now, this is too much, I don't even want this anymore." But even though I'm thinking that, it feels like the actual decision has just completely slipped out of my hands. 

It's like someone else is driving the car, you know? My hands just keep moving, bringing the food to my mouth, ripping open the next carton, and my brain is just trapped in the passenger seat watching it all happen. I'll want to stop, I really will, but the physical ability to just put the fork down or push the bag away... it's just gone. I can't do it. It's so incredibly frustrating because I know I'm a capable person. I manage complex design projects, I handle difficult clients, I run my own life... but in those moments, staring at my screen with all those empty containers piling up, I have absolutely zero agency over my own actions. I just can't stop until it's all gone.

I... hmm. Let me really think about that for a second. Because obviously, life is stressful, right? It's not like my job is the absolute only thing in the world that ever goes wrong or causes me anxiety. 

Like, just to give you an example, last year my boyfriend and I broke up after three years together, and that was... I mean, it was just devastating. It was incredibly stressful, having to untangle our lives, figure out who was keeping the apartment, splitting up the furniture, all of that emotional heavy lifting. And you would think, if stress was just this universal trigger for me to eat, that I would have been eating everything in sight during that whole process. But I wasn't. I actually... I just ate completely normally. Maybe even a little less than normal because I was sad. It wasn't that same frantic, out-of-control feeling at all. 

Or, oh, here's another one—when my sister had a pretty serious health scare a few months ago. That was absolutely terrifying. I was pacing the waiting room at the hospital, just completely overwhelmed, sick to my stomach with worry. But the thought of ordering a bunch of takeout or eating past the point of being full? It literally never even crossed my mind. In those kinds of personal situations, my stomach actually gets tied up in knots and I don't want food at all. 

It's so weird, isn't it? Because stress is stress, right? Like, biologically speaking, your body is just releasing cortisol whether it's a breakup or a deadline. But for some reason, the stress of a looming design project, the pressure of a client hating a logo I spent forty hours perfecting... that specific type of professional, performance-based anxiety is the only thing that flips that switch in my brain. I've analyzed this so much myself, trying to figure out if maybe I'm just a stress-eater across the board, but I really can't find a single instance outside of my freelance work where I cope by eating like that. 

It's almost like my brain has entirely different filing cabinets for how to handle different types of panic. Personal life panic means I cry and call my mom or pace around. But professional panic? That means I buy sixty dollars worth of Chinese food and completely lose myself in it. So... no, I really can't think of any situation outside of work where this happens. Which honestly just makes the whole thing even more confusing to me, because if it was just a general stress response, that would almost make more sense, you know? But it's just so hyper-specific to my desk and my deadlines.

Oh, I try. I try so hard. I mean... it's not like I want to be doing this, right? I set up all these rules for myself constantly. I'll tell myself, "Okay, tonight you're just going to have a normal dinner, you'll eat your meal prep, and then you'll close the kitchen." I've even tried putting sticky notes on my fridge, or installing those website blockers on my computer so I can't get onto UberEats or DoorDash after 8 PM when I'm working late. I really, really try to put up roadblocks because I know how awful I'm going to feel afterward, physically and mentally. 

But when that specific deadline dread hits... it's like all those rules just completely evaporate. I'll find a way around the app blockers, or I'll just walk straight into the kitchen. And the scariest part is what happens next, because once I start, there’s this point where I’m basically just watching myself keep clicking back to the food, or opening another package of whatever I found in the cupboard, and I'm actively thinking I should stop. My inner voice is literally saying, "You don't need this, you're full, just put it down." But it feels like the decision has already completely slipped out of my hands. 

It's almost like an out-of-body experience. I'm a passenger in my own body, just watching my hands move, watching myself unwrap another thing or take another bite. And it's so incredibly frustrating because I'm a capable person, you know? I run my own freelance business, I manage complex projects, I make hundreds of micro-decisions about color theory and layout all day long. I am in control of my professional life. But when it comes to just stopping myself from eating when that work panic sets in? I have absolutely zero control. The rational part of my brain is still awake, still telling me to stop, but the physical part of me just overrides it completely until the food is gone.

I can say, \"Oh, it's just the pressure of this branding package, it's just the client being demanding.\" If the stress is completely gone and I still lose control like that, then what's my excuse? Personal life panic means I cry and call my mom or pace around. But professional panic? That means I buy sixty dollars worth of Chinese food and completely lose myself in it. So... no, I really can't think of any situation outside of work where this happens. Once I start, there's this point where I'm literally just watching myself keep clicking back to the food, or reaching out and tearing open another plastic package, and my internal monologue is completely disconnected from what my body is doing. I'm sitting there actively thinking, \"I should stop. I really need to stop right now, this is too much, I don't even want this anymore.\" But even though I'm thinking that, it feels like the actual decision has just completely slipped out of my hands. \n\nIt's like someone else is driving the car, you know? My hands just keep moving, bringing the food to my mouth, ripping open the next carton, and my brain is just trapped in the passenger seat watching it all happen. I'll want to stop, I really will, but the physical ability to just put the fork down or push the bag away... it's just gone. I can't do it. It's so incredibly frustrating because I know I'm a capable person. I manage complex design projects, I handle difficult clients, I run my own life... but in those moments, staring at my screen with all those empty containers piling up, I have absolutely zero agency over my own actions. I just can't stop until it's all gone.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive eating would stop if your work-related stress was significantly reduced or eliminated?\n\nPatient: I... gosh, I really don't know. I mean, I want to say yes, right? Because we've just spent all this time talking about how it only happens when I'm stressed about a design deadline. Logically, it makes sense. If you take away the deadline, you take away the eating. \n\nBut... I don't know if I can say for sure, because I start thinking about what it would actually mean to significantly reduce my work stress, and it just feels impossible to even picture. I'm a freelance graphic designer. My entire livelihood is based on finding the next client, pleasing the current client, making sure the typography is absolutely perfect, and getting the files to the printer by 8 AM. The stress is just... it's baked into the career. It's the water I swim in. So trying to imagine a version of my life where that stress is just eliminated? It's almost like trying to imagine living on another planet. \n\nAnd honestly, there's a part of me that's actually really terrified to find out the answer to your question. Because what if I did take a break? What if I took a month off, or I somehow found this magical, low-stress in-house job where I just clocked out at 5 PM every day, and I was totally relaxed... and then I still found myself sitting at my desk at midnight surrounded by empty takeout containers? That's a really scary thought. Because right now, I can blame the job. I can say, \"Oh, it's just the pressure of this branding package, it's just the client being demanding.\" If the stress is completely gone and I still lose control like that, then what's my excuse? Then it's just me, you know? \n\nSo, I guess... I really just don't know. I hope it would stop. I really, really hope it would. Because the logic says it should, since they feel so completely connected to each other right now. But since I haven't had a truly stress-free period in my career since I graduated, I've never actually been in a position to test that theory. I just... I can't give you a definitive yes or no. I wish I could, I really do, but I just don't know what would happen.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation, regardless of work, where you felt extremely stressed or overwhelmed and turned to eating excessively as a result?\n\nPatient: I... hmm. Let me really think about that for a second. Because obviously, life is stressful, right? It's not like my job is the absolute only thing in the world that ever goes wrong or causes me anxiety. \n\nLike, just to give you an example, last year my boyfriend and I broke up after three years together, and that was... I mean, it was just devastating. It was incredibly stressful, having to untangle our lives, figure out who was keeping the apartment, splitting up the furniture, all of that emotional heavy lifting. And you would think, if stress was just this universal trigger for me to eat, that I would have been eating everything in sight during that whole process. But I wasn't. I actually... It wasn't that same frantic, out-of-control feeling at all. \n\nOr, oh, here's another one—when my sister had a pretty serious health scare a few months ago. That was absolutely terrifying. I was pacing the waiting room at the hospital, just completely overwhelmed, sick to my stomach with worry. But the thought of ordering a bunch of takeout or eating past the point of being full? It literally never even crossed my mind. In those kinds of personal situations, my stomach actually gets tied up in knots and I don't want food at all. \n\nIt's so weird, isn't it? Because stress is stress, right? Like, biologically speaking, your body is just releasing cortisol whether it's a breakup or a deadline. But for some reason, the stress of a looming design project, the pressure of a client hating a logo I spent forty hours perfecting... that specific type of professional, performance-based anxiety is the only thing that flips that switch in my brain. I've analyzed this so much myself, trying to figure out if maybe I'm just a stress-eater across the board, but I really can't find a single instance outside of my freelance work where I cope by eating like that. \n\nIt's almost like my brain has entirely different filing cabinets for how to handle different types of panic. Personal life panic means I cry and call my mom or pace around. But professional panic? That means I buy sixty dollars worth of Chinese food and completely lose myself in it. So... no, I really can't think of any situation outside of work where this happens. Which honestly just makes the whole thing even more confusing to me, because if it was just a general stress response, that would almost make more sense, you know? But it's just so hyper-specific to my desk and my deadlines.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive eating is a way to cope with stress in general, or is it specifically related to the stress you experience from work?\n\nPatient: I mean, based on everything I just laid out, it really has to be specifically related to the work stress. I know it probably sounds a bit bizarre, because, like I was saying earlier, stress is stress, right? But... yeah, it's just the work. I've spent so many hours just sitting on my couch, staring at the ceiling, trying to psychoanalyze myself and figure out if there's some hidden pattern I'm missing. Like, do I do this when I get a parking ticket? Do I do this when I have a disagreement with a friend? And the answer is always no. It is entirely, one hundred percent tied to my job. \n\nThere's just something about the specific kind of pressure that comes with freelance design. It's not just having a lot to do. It's this crushing weight of knowing that my entire livelihood depends on my ability to be perfectly creative on demand. You know? Like, a client wants a whole new brand identity by Friday, and they want it to be totally groundbreaking, and I'm sitting there at 11 PM staring at a blank artboard on my monitor, and the cursor is just blinking at me, and I feel this absolute dread in the pit of my stomach. That specific dread? That's the trigger. That's the exact moment my brain decides we need to order enough Thai food for four people and just eat until the physical discomfort outweighs the mental panic. \n\nIf I'm stressed about, I don't know, my rent going up, or getting a flat tire, I might complain about it, I might cry, I might call my mom and vent for two hours, but I don't eat. I don't get that frantic, out-of-body urge to just consume everything in my kitchen. It really is just this bizarre, isolated response to my professional life. But yeah, to answer your question, it's definitely not general stress. It's the work. It's always just the work.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever tried to stop or control your excessive eating when you're stressed about work?\n\nPatient: Oh, I try. I try so hard. I mean... it's not like I want to be doing this, right? I set up all these rules for myself constantly. I'll tell myself, \"Okay, tonight you're just going to have a normal dinner, you'll eat your meal prep, and then you'll close the kitchen.\" I've even tried putting sticky notes on my fridge, or installing those website blockers on my computer so I can't get onto UberEats or DoorDash after 8 PM when I'm working late. I really, really try to put up roadblocks because I know how awful I'm going to feel afterward, physically and mentally. \n\nBut when that specific deadline dread hits... it's like all those rules just completely evaporate. I'll find a way around the app blockers, or I'll just walk straight into the kitchen. And the scariest part is what happens next, because once I start, there’s this point where I’m basically just watching myself keep clicking back to the food, or opening another package of whatever I found in the cupboard, and I'm actively thinking I should stop. My inner voice is literally saying, \"You don't need this, you're full, just put it down.\" But it feels like the decision has already completely slipped out of my hands. \n\nIt's almost like an out-of-body experience. I'm a passenger in my own body, just watching my hands move, watching myself unwrap another thing or take another bite. And it's so incredibly frustrating because I'm a capable person, you know? I run my own freelance business, I manage complex projects, I make hundreds of micro-decisions about color theory and layout all day long. I am in control of my professional life. But when it comes to just stopping myself from eating when that work panic sets in? I have absolutely zero control. The rational part of my brain is still awake, still telling me to stop, but the physical part of me just overrides it completely until the food is gone.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever sought help or talked to someone about your excessive eating episodes?\n\nPatient: I... no.
